translations.title: All Systems Go
translations.explanation: A linear system can be represented compactly by a matrix equation A x=b. Each row of the coefficient matrix A holds the coefficients from one equation, and the variable column x must use the same variable order throughout. An augmented matrix [A|b] records the system for elimination. Elementary row operations produce an equivalent system: exchange rows, multiply a row by a nonzero constant, or replace a row by itself plus a multiple of another row. Row reduction distinguishes a unique solution from infinitely many solutions and inconsistent systems. When A is square and invertible, the solution is x=A⁻¹b; if A is singular there is no such inverse and row reduction must be interpreted directly.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: For x+y+z=6, 2x−y+z=3, x+2y−z=2, the matrix equation is [[1,1,1],[2,−1,1],[1,2,−1]]·[x,y,z]ᵀ=[6,3,2]ᵀ. Legal row operations are Ri↔Rj; Ri←kRi with k≠0; and Ri←Ri+kRj. A row [0,0,0|c] with c≠0 means inconsistency; a zero row with free variables may indicate multiple solutions. For invertible square A, multiplying Ax=b by A⁻¹ yields x=A⁻¹b. Matrix multiplication order matters: A⁻¹b, not bA⁻¹.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — solve a 3×3 system: form [1 1 1|6; 2 −1 1|3; 1 2 −1|2]. Apply R₂←R₂−2R₁ to obtain [0 −3 −1|−9]; apply R₃←R₃−R₁ to obtain [0 1 −2|−4]. Then R₂←R₂+3R₃ gives [0 0 −7|−21], so z=3. Back-substitute y−2(3)=−4 to get y=2 and x+2+3=6 to get x=1. Verify in all three original equations: 6, 3, and 2. Example 2 — inconsistent system: x+y=2 and 2x+2y=5 produce a row [0,0|1] after subtracting twice row 1; no solution exists.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Choose and label the variable order; transcribe all coefficient signs correctly into A and constants into b. 2. Write [A|b] and select a nonzero pivot (swap rows if needed). 3. Use legal operations to eliminate entries under successive pivots. 4. Continue to echelon or reduced echelon form and interpret zero rows before claiming uniqueness. 5. Back-substitute or read variable values from reduced echelon form. 6. Substitute the proposed values in EVERY original equation. 7. If using A⁻¹b instead, independently verify that A is square/invertible and that Ax=b.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not reorder variables between equations or lose negative signs in the augmented matrix. Multiplying a row by zero destroys equivalence. A row such as [0,0|1] signifies a contradiction, not a new variable. Not every square matrix is invertible. Do not confuse matrix multiplication with componentwise multiplication, and do not compute bA⁻¹ where dimensions or order are wrong. Always check solutions in the original system.
translations.quickSummary: Represent a linear system as Ax=b and [A|b], reduce rows using equivalence-preserving operations, classify solution count and check in the original equations. Use x=A⁻¹b only when A is invertible.

translations.title: Log Logic
translations.explanation: A logarithm answers an exponent question. For a base b>0 with b≠1, y=log_b(x) means exactly bʸ=x, so exponential and logarithmic functions are inverses. Logarithms are defined only for x>0 in the real number system. Their graphs reflect exponential graphs across y=x: the exponential curve passes through (0,1), while its inverse logarithm passes through (1,0). The logarithm is increasing when b>1 and decreasing when 0<b<1. Use a logarithm when a variable is in the exponent, and check the domain before accepting a solution.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Inverse identity: log_b(bˣ)=x for real x, and b^(log_b x)=x for x>0; b>0 and b≠1. log_b 1=0, log_b b=1. A logarithmic function has domain x>0, range all real numbers, and vertical asymptote x=0. For b>1 it grows; for 0<b<1 it decreases. log_b(xy)=log_b x+log_b y applies only for x,y>0; log_b(x+y) generally does NOT split into a sum. Change of base: log_b x=ln(x)/ln(b) for x>0 and valid b.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: log₂(32)=5 because 2⁵=32. Example 2: log₃(1/9)=−2 because 3⁻²=1/9. Example 3: solve log₂(x)=−3. Rewrite 2⁻³=x, so x=1/8; checking log₂(1/8)=−3 verifies it. Example 4: solve 2ˣ=7. The inverse gives x=log₂ 7=ln 7/ln 2≈2.807; substituting gives approximately 7. Graph the matching points (3,8) on y=2ˣ and (8,3) on y=log₂ x, which are reflections over y=x.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the base b and verify b>0, b≠1. 2. Convert log_b(x)=y into bʸ=x, or convert bʸ=x into log_b(x)=y. 3. Solve the equivalent equation using known powers or the change-of-base formula as appropriate. 4. Check that every logarithm input is strictly positive; discard extraneous answers. 5. If interpreting a graph, exchange input/output coordinates across the line y=x and label the logarithmic vertical asymptote. 6. Check your answer by evaluating the corresponding exponential form.
translations.commonMistakes: log_b(x) is an exponent, not b×x or x/b. Negative LOGARITHM VALUES are permitted, but logarithm inputs must be positive. Bases cannot equal 0, 1, or a negative real number in this context. The false rule log_b(x+y)=log_b x+log_b y must not be used. Inverse notation does not mean taking a reciprocal. An exponential has a horizontal asymptote; its logarithmic inverse has a vertical one.
translations.quickSummary: log_b x=y ↔ bʸ=x for b>0, b≠1 and x>0. Exponential and logarithmic graphs reflect across y=x. Use inverse operations to solve exponent equations and check the logarithm's positive input.
